All images were studied, and the number of individuals in each image, where they were, was counted. It is necessary to calculate the abundance of marine mammls and build a map with environmental covariates (ice conditions, depth, etc).

I just can't figure out how to use distance to solve this problem. After all, we do not have a detection function in this case?

Probably a similar question has been discussed before, but I couldn't find it. I will be very grateful for your advice!

Sincerely

Sergey

messages.body_plain:
Sergey

Depending upon how the images were taken (for example, looking vertically to the water) so that detectability is perfect from the centre to the edge of the images, then it is not a distance sampling problem.  Distance sampling is used to determine the probability of detection given that detectability is perfect on the flight line and diminishes with distance from the flight line.

Instead, you have what is called a "strip transect" where all animals within the strip are detected.  However an added complication is whether you are counting detections only of animals on the surface or are animals under the surface being detected.  That raises issues of availability to be detected.

You may want to consult the following papers:

Stevenson, BC, Borchers, DL, Fewster, RM. Cluster capture-recapture to account for identification uncertainty on aerial surveys of animal populations. Biometrics. 2018; 1– 11.  https://doi.org/10.1111/biom.12983

Buckland, S.T., Burt, M.L., Rexstad, E.A., Mellor, M., Williams, A.E. and Woodward, R. (2012), Aerial surveys of seabirds: the advent of digital methods. Journal of Applied Ecology, 49: 960-967. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2012.02150.x  [this deals with seabirds and strip transect analysis, does not address animal availability]

messages.subject_clean: is it possible to include radial distances in distance sampling with line transects
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to use distance sampling as a method to analyze bird abundance data from line transects (using RStudio, not the program Distance). I have 15 line transects each repeated 3 times with the design being that 2 observers started at the mid-point and walk out to the end point. The 15 transects are from 3 plots with 5 sites (Study.Area) (each site being a different treatment that is repeated among plots). So I have 5 treatments repeated 3 times.

I understand that for line transects, the "distance" used is the perpendicular distance of the bird observed to the observer. But I have estimates of the radial distance of the bird to the center based on distance of the observer to the center, bearing of the bird from the observer, and estimated distance of the bird from the observer.

I want to know how abundance might change by treatment (Region.Label) with increased distance from the center, hence why I have these radial distances. But when I use formula = ~radial_distance, I get errors.

Is this question achievable with distance sampling?

Other questions that are slightly related. Can I include site as a random variable in these analyses? Can I look at an interaction between treatment and radial distance, or include interactions at all?

Previous students I know have used GLMMs to estimate abundance in the same study system as I am referring to, but I want to use distance sampling if I can as it seems to be very popular for estimating abundance and I appreciate the inclusion of detectability as my transects were performed by observers of different bird ID skill levels.

I am happy to include some of my code, or show what my raw data looks like if these questions don't make sense or need to be clarified. I am relatively new to R and performing statistical analyses, and all my work using distance sampling has been self-taught, so any help is greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!!

Johanna

messages.body_plain:
Johanna

I think I understand your study design with 5 treatments therefore you would like to estimate bird abundance for each of these treatments.  I think you have three transects for each of the treatments, which is a small level of replication on which to base your abundance estimates.

I'm troubled by your statement "how abundance might change by treatment (Region.Label) with increased distance from the center".  This makes me think you believe abundance changes as a function of distance along the transect (transects being walked outward from the centre).  This makes your problem difficult for distance sampling because a) estimation of abundance requires multiple transects and b) using ~radial.distance in the detection function model simply states that detectability changes as a function of distance to the centre.  If both detectability and abundance are changing from the centre, they are confounded and analysis is not possible without further data.

Distance sampling does account for imperfect detectability, but to do so, sufficient detections need to be made and sufficient spatial replication of transects are needed for each stratum (treatment) for which you wish to estimate abundance.  My sense is that your design does not lend itself to analysis via distance sampling.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance users,

I have two questions.

1.
I wish to estimate cluster size bias in a
population that was surveyed using line transects, and use this size bias to correct
for cluster sizes observed in a neighbor population.

I would follow the following procedure.

I first extract an estimation of expected cluster size
(CSexp) from the summary of the retained DS model.

I also have the observed mean cluster size (CSobs) for each
of my species.

Then, to estimate the relative bias associated with cluster
size estimation, I use:

Relative Bias = (CSobs – CSexp) / CSexp

Next, I apply this relative bias to each cluster size
observed in the neighbor site where we have line transects for which we tried
to estimate distances, but unfortunately, distance data are not satisfactory.
Thus we do not have distance data for that neighbor site. Then I use the
equation 3.2 provided in Buckland et al. (2001) (page 51) to estimate density :

D = E(n)*E(s)/(a*Pa), with E(n) the expected number of
clusters, E(s) the expectation of cluster size for the population, a the area
covered by the survey and Pa the probability of detection for an object within
this area.

Would this approach be correct ?

Also, the ‘cluster size’ covariate is not always retained in
the most supported DS model. In that case, does that mean there is no size
bias, and thus, we would not need to correct for cluster sizes obtained for the
neighboor site to estimate densities ?

2.
Question regarding Eqn 3.2 and 3.3 of Buckland
et al. (2001) – page 51

 To estimate densities for species in the neighbor site, I
use Equation 3.2 presented page 51 of Buckland et al. (2001), which uses E(n),
the expected number of clusters in the surveyed area.

To me, the estimator of E(n) would be n, the total number of
clusters sampled in the surveyed area. This number is a fixed number in my
dataset, as I have a unique and precise number of clusters that were observed.
However, page 52 of the book provides the equation (3.4) that is based notably
on the variance of n. However, I do not understand how we can have a variance
associated to n, as this number is fixed in our dataset.

There is probably something that I am missing here, but I
cannot understand what, and I would greatly appreciate your help to better
understand those equations and how to implement them for my data.

Many thanks in advance for your help.

Cheers,

Delphine

This seems OK, though you seem to be making it more complicated than necessary.  Assuming CSexp was calculated adjusting for size bias, then you can just take E(s) from the neighbouring site and multiply it by CSexp/CSobs.  A couple of provisos here.  First, you must assume that the data from the neighbouring site are similar to those from the first site, so that you can assume the same correction factor applies.  Second, you should estimate the contribution to variance of this correction factor, for example using a bootstrap.
Your n is the observed sample size.  If you were to repeat the same survey, you would observe a different n.  Thus it is not fixed.  (Contrast this with L, which if you repeat the first survey using the same design, would remain unchanged.)

Steve Buckland

1.      Thank you for your explanation. Indeed, I may have complicated things more than necessary and I will use the method you suggest. About the variance, cannot we propagate the variance of the different estimators (E(s), Csexp and Csobs) using the delta method ? Could you explain me otherwise why it is better to use a bootstrap ?

The delta method could be used, but the problem is that Csexp and Csobs cannot be assumed to be independent – you would overestimate variance if you assume they are.

2.      For n, I understand what you mean, but in my case, the survey was performed only once. Then, how can I calculate a variance for n if I only have one "replicate" for this survey ?

If you want to draw inference on a wider area, you need to have a design that has replicate lines through the study area.  We use variation in encounter rate among lines to estimate variance in n.  If you have only a single line, inference is restricted to the single strip you surveyed.  In that case, you might assume that N is distributed as Poisson, with var(n)=E(n), estimated by n.  This generally underestimates true variance, as most natural populations are overdispersed relative to Poisson.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Dear distance samplers,

We are pleased to announce the release of a new version of Distance for Windows, Distance 7.4. This version features some enhancements to facilitate the analysis of camera trap distance sampling (CTDS) data. These enhancements include:
new Project Setup Wizard option to create projects tailored for CTDS analysis
ability to incorporate uncertainty in activity multiplier via non-parametric bootstrap
new model selection criterion: QAIC
new chapter in the online help documenting how to undertake CTDS analysis
new sample project illustrating CTDS analysis of duiker data

The ability to incorporate uncertainty in multipliers via the bootstrap is general, and so potentially of use in other applications. It requires the user to import a set of bootstrap replicate values for each multiplier. For more details, see the Distance help.

There are a few other minor improvements and bug fixes. We have also taken the opportunity to include the latest version of the R packages underlying the MRDS, DSM and MA analysis engines, and the simulation functionality.

One important aspect of CTDS analysis is determining the proportion of time animals are active during the diurnal period of the survey. To facilitate analysis of activity data, we have built a graphical, web-based interface to the activity package in R. A link to this is given on the Distance project home page (http://distancesampling.org/ - see "Activity interface" on the left side of that page). We expect to move the interface to a local site once we have an appropriate server up and running, and will update the link in due course.

We thank the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) for a grant that enabled the design of the new CTDS functionality. We had previously undertaken to maintain Distance for Windows but not to add new functionality -- the increasing use of distance sampling in camera trap applications, and the generous support of WCS changed our mind!

We are planning another release of Distance for Windows (version 7.5) for summer 2022. This will be a maintenance release, containing no new features, but a move to a more modern installer that we expect to work better on the latest versions of Windows.

With best wishes to all,

Distance Development Team

Centre for Research into Ecological & Environmental Modelling

University of St. Andrews

messages.body_plain:
Sylvia

Thanks for your clarification that you are using Distance for Windows.  Studying your data, I see that you are analysing pellet count data for roe deer.  You have recorded the number of pellets in each pellet group you detected; is that correct?

When you created your Distance for Windows project, I suspect you ticked the box that said "clusters of objects"

For pellet surveys, this is not what you want to do.  Your analysis will consist of estimating the density of pellet groups in your study area, then you will estimate the number of pellet groups produced per deer per day as well as the rate at which pellet groups decay.  As you see, the focus is on the pellet group, not individual pellets.

You can still have number of pellets in your project, perhaps to use as a covariate that influences detectability along with distance from transect.  But because you ticked "clusters of objects", Distance for Windows is treating the number of pellets in a particular way that is causing difficulties.

Create a new project and tick "single objects", I think that will resolve your problems.  Let me know if you have other questions.
